knowledge:
- key_parameters: aC=A list containing the atomic composition of the substance (e.g., list(C=50, H=71, N=13, O=12, S=0)) ;; nrPeaks=The number of consecutive aggregated isotopic variants to calculate ;; stopOption=The stopping criterion for probability calculations, which can be "coverage" or "abundantEstim" ;; coverage=The cumulative probability threshold (e.g., 0.99) used when stopOption is "coverage" ;; abundantEstim=The abundance threshold (e.g., 10) used when stopOption is "abundantEstim" ;; approxParam=The RCL (Recurrence of Constant Length) approximation parameter in useBRAIN2 (values >= 5 are recommended) ;; approxStart=The LSP (Late Starting Point) approximation parameter in useBRAIN2 to narrow down computations to peak indices around the most abundant ones
- alternatives: None mentioned, but the package is presented as a computation- and memory-efficient alternative to traditional combinatorial methods that suffer from combinatorial explosion for large molecules.
- when_to_use: Use this package when analyzing mass spectrometry data in proteomics to calculate theoretical isotopic distributions, monoisotopic masses, and average masses of peptides or proteins to interpret complex spectral patterns.
- pitfalls: For extremely large atomic configurations, numerical problems may occur, which can be handled by checking if the calculated monoisotopic mass is NA. The LSP (Late Starting Point) approximation requires a burn-in period to retrieve accurate isotopic ratios, with a suggested rule-of-thumb burn-in of ceiling(log10(monoisotopicMass)) + 5.

workflows.name: single_molecule_isotopic_distribution
workflows.intent: Calculate and plot the aggregated isotopic distribution, monoisotopic mass, and average mass for a single chemical substance or peptide sequence.
input: chemical_composition.txt (A list or table defining the atomic counts of C, H, N, O, and S for the target molecule)
workflows.stages: 1. Define the atomic composition list ;; 2. Calculate the theoretical monoisotopic mass ;; 3. Calculate the theoretical average mass ;; 4. Estimate the required number of peaks ;; 5. Compute isotopic probabilities with various stopping criteria ;; 6. Run the global useBRAIN function to obtain masses and abundances for plotting
workflows.code:
angiotensineII <- list(C=50,H=71,N=13,O=12) 
monoisotopicMassAngiotensineII <- calculateMonoisotopicMass(aC = angiotensineII)
monoisotopicMassAngiotensineII
averageMassAngiotensineII <- calculateAverageMass(aC = angiotensineII)
averageMassAngiotensineII
nrPeaksAngiotensineII <- calculateNrPeaks(aC = angiotensineII)
nrPeaksAngiotensineII
prob1 <- calculateIsotopicProbabilities(aC = angiotensineII)
prob2 <- calculateIsotopicProbabilities(aC = angiotensineII, nrPeaks=20)
prob3 <- calculateIsotopicProbabilities(aC = angiotensineII, stopOption = "coverage", coverage = 0.99)
prob4 <- calculateIsotopicProbabilities(aC = angiotensineII, stopOption = "abundantEstim", abundantEstim = 10)
res <- useBRAIN(aC= angiotensineII)

workflows.name: high_throughput_protein_processing
workflows.intent: Process a tabular file of protein sequences to calculate atomic compositions, monoisotopic masses, and most abundant peak masses in high-throughput.
input: uniprot.tab (A tab-delimited text file containing protein sequences under a "Sequence" column)
workflows.stages: 1. Read and clean the protein sequence data ;; 2. Filter sequences to ensure they only contain the 20 standard amino acids ;; 3. Convert amino acid sequences to atomic compositions ;; 4. Calculate isotopic distributions and extract monoisotopic and most abundant peak masses ;; 5. Export the processed data to a text file
workflows.code:
tabUniprot <- read.table('data/uniprot.tab', sep="\t", header=TRUE) 
tabUniprot$Sequence <- gsub(" ", "", tabUniprot$Sequence)
howMany <- nrow(tabUniprot)
AMINOS <- c("A", "R", "N", "D", "C", "E", "Q", "G", "H", "I", "L", "K", "M", "F", "P", "S", "T", "W", "Y", "V")
nrPeaks = 1000
dfUniprot <- data.frame()
for (idx in 1:howMany){
  seq <- as.character(tabUniprot[idx,"Sequence"])
  seqVector <- strsplit(seq, split="")[[1]]
  if (!is.na(sum(match(seqVector, AMINOS)))){  
  aC <- getAtomsFromSeq(seq)
  res <- useBRAIN(aC = aC, nrPeaks = nrPeaks, stopOption = "abundantEstim", abundantEstim = 10)
  isoDistr <- res$isoDistr
  masses <- res$masses
  maxIdx <- which.max(isoDistr)
  mostAbundantPeakMass <- masses[maxIdx]
  monoMass <- res$monoisotopicMass  
  dfAtomicComp <- data.frame(C=aC[1], H=aC[2], N=aC[3], O=aC[4], S=aC[5])
  singleDfUniprot <- data.frame(dfAtomicComp, monoMass=monoMass, maxIdx=maxIdx, mostAbundantPeakMass=mostAbundantPeakMass)
  if (!is.na(monoMass)){ #for huge atomic configuration numerical problems may occur
    dfUniprot <- rbind(dfUniprot, singleDfUniprot)
  }
  }
}
write.table(unique(dfUniprot), "data/uniprotBRAIN.txt")

workflows.name: heuristic_isotopic_distribution
workflows.intent: Compute isotopic distributions for large molecules using time- and memory-saving heuristics (RCL and LSP) via BRAIN 2.0.
input: large_molecule_composition.txt (Atomic composition list of a large biomolecule)
workflows.stages: 1. Define the atomic composition ;; 2. Run useBRAIN2 with the RCL (Recurrence of Constant Length) approximation using approxParam ;; 3. Run useBRAIN2 with the LSP (Late Starting Point) approximation using approxStart to focus on the most abundant peak region
workflows.code:
resNoRCL <-  useBRAIN2(aC = aC, nrPeaks = nrPeaks)$iso
resRCL   <-  useBRAIN2(aC = aC, nrPeaks = nrPeaks, approxParam = 10)$iso
resNoLSP <-  useBRAIN2(aC = aC, nrPeaks = endIdx)$iso
resLSP   <-  useBRAIN2(aC = aC, nrPeaks = endIdx, approxStart = approxStart)$iso
